loText: Calculate the short-term rate change and describe the basis point volatility using the CIR and lognormal models.
question: A rates desk calibrates three short-rate models so that each gives a basis-point volatility of 100 bp when the short rate is 8%: a normal model (constant basis-point volatility), the CIR model (basis-point volatility $\sigma\sqrt{r}$) and a lognormal model (basis-point volatility $\sigma r$). The parameters are then held fixed while the short rate falls to 2%. Which of the following is closest to the basis-point volatilities of the CIR model and of the lognormal model at the 2% rate?

options.A: CIR 25 bp; lognormal 50 bp
options.B: CIR 50 bp; lognormal 25 bp
options.C: CIR 100 bp; lognormal 100 bp
options.D: CIR 200 bp; lognormal 400 bp

solution:
**Step 1 – Calibrate at 8%**

$$\sigma_{CIR}\sqrt{0.08} = 0.01 \Rightarrow\sigma_{CIR} = 0.035355 \sigma_{Y} \times0.08 = 0.01 \Rightarrow\sigma_{Y} = 0.125$$

**Step 2 – Re-evaluate at 2%**

CIR: $0.035355 \times\sqrt{0.02} = 0.0050 = 50$ bp Lognormal: 0.125 × 0.02 = 0.0025 = 25 bp

⇒ Equivalently, CIR scales by $\sqrt{2/8} = 0.5$ and the lognormal by 2/8 = 0.25.

**Interpretation**

When rates fall, the lognormal model’s basis-point volatility shrinks fastest, CIR’s more slowly, and the normal model’s not at all (Figure 1). In yield-volatility terms CIR is now at 50/200 = 25% while the lognormal stays at 12.5%.

**LO:** MR-15 e: Calculate the short-term rate change and describe the basis point volatility using the CIR and lognormal models. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.15, 15.2, eqs. 15.6 to 15.8 and Figure 15.2

MR-15 • The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

loText: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion.
question: A junior quant describes the lognormal model with deterministic drift (the “Salomon Brothers” model), $dr = a(t) r dt + \sigma r dw$, to a model validation committee. Which of the following descriptions is correct?

options.A: The natural logarithm of the short rate follows a Ho-Lee-type process with a time-dependent drift, so the short rate is lognormal and every node of its tree is positive.
options.B: The natural logarithm of the short rate reverts toward a time-dependent central tendency ln $\theta(t)$, so the short rate is lognormal and every node of its tree is positive.
options.C: The short rate follows a Ho-Lee-type process with a time-dependent drift, so the short rate is normal and low nodes of its tree may become negative.
options.D: The basis-point volatility of the short rate is proportional to the square root of the rate, so the short rate is non-negative but not lognormal.

solution:
**Step 1 – Apply Ito’s lemma**

$d[\text{ln} r] = [a(t) - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}] dt + \sigma dw = a\tilde{(} t) dt + \sigma dw$: a Ho-Lee process written on ln $r$.

**Step 2 – Consequences**

ln $r$ is normal, so $r$ is lognormal; nodes are $r_{0}\text{e}^{(\cdot)} > 0$.

⇒ “The Ho-Lee model based on the natural logarithm of the short rate.”

**Interpretation**

The drift is deterministic and time-dependent (fitted to bond prices), with no mean reversion. That is what separates it from Black-Karasinski.

**LO:** MR-15 f: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.15, 15.3, eqs. 15.9 to 15.12

loText: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion.
question: In a lognormal short-rate tree with $a_{1} = 0$ and $dt = 1$, the up node after one period is $r_{0} \text{e}^{\sigma}$. The model’s volatility parameter is $\sigma= 12.5\%$ and the current short rate is 4.00%. Which statement best explains why volatility in this model is quoted as a percentage of the rate?

options.A: Because e$^{\sigma} \approx1 + \sigma$, the up-state rate is about 12.5% above the current rate, about 4.5%, so the size of the move scales with the level of the rate.
options.B: Because e$^{\sigma} \approx1 + \sigma$, the up-state rate is about 12.5 percentage points above the current rate, about 16.5%, so the size of the move is fixed in basis points.
options.C: Because the drift is additive, the up-state rate is the current rate plus 12.5% of the long-run level, so the size of the move scales with the long-run level.
options.D: Because the tree is built in rates rather than in logs, the up-state rate is the current rate times 12.5%, so the size of the move scales with the level of the rate.

solution:
**Step 1 – Use the small-**$x$ **approximation**

$r_{0}\text{e}^{\sigma} \approx r_{0}(1 + \sigma) = 4.00\% \times1.125 = 4.50\%$ (exactly $4.00\% \times\text{e}^{0.125} = 4.53\%$).

**Step 2 – Interpret**

The move is 12.5% of the rate, about 50 bp here. At a 2% rate the same $\sigma$ would move it by about 25 bp.

⇒ Volatility is a percentage of the rate: yield volatility.

**Interpretation**

GARP: “Volatility is clearly a percentage of the rate…If, for example, $\sigma= 12.5\%$, then the short rate in the up-state is 12.5% above the initial short rate.”

**LO:** MR-15 f: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.15, 15.3, eq. 15.13

loText: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion.
question: A Black-Karasinski tree with a fixed time step $dt$ recombines only if $k(2) =$ $[\sigma(1) - \sigma(2)] / [\sigma(1) dt]$. Instead of imposing this restriction, the model lets the length of the time step vary. Which of the following best explains why?

options.A: Mean reversion controls the term structure of volatility while time-dependent volatility controls the future volatility of the short rate, so the two must be chosen independently.
options.B: Mean reversion controls the future volatility of the short rate while time-dependent volatility controls the term structure of volatility, so the two must be chosen independently.
options.C: Imposing the restriction would make the model an equilibrium model, while varying the time step keeps the drift deterministic and removes mean reversion.
options.D: Varying the time step always makes the tree recombine, whatever mean reversion and volatility functions are chosen, so no restriction on $dt_{2}$ is needed.

solution:
**Step 1 – What the restriction would do**

Imposing $k(2) = [\sigma(1) - \sigma(2)]/[\sigma(1)dt]$ “would require that the mean reversion speed be completely determined by the time-dependent volatility function.”

**Step 2 – Why that is unacceptable**

The two serve distinct purposes: mean reversion controls the term structure of volatility; time-dependent volatility controls the future volatility of the short rate, and hence the prices of options expiring at different times.

⇒ Letting $dt$ vary keeps both free.

**Interpretation**

The length of the first step is arbitrary; the second is set to satisfy eq. 15.23.

**LO:** MR-15 f: Describe lognormal models with deterministic drift and mean reversion. • **Reference:** GARP MR Ch.15, 15.4

loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
question: A fixed-income analyst calibrates Tuckman’s Model 1 (normal rates, no drift) with $r_{0} = 6.18\%$ and $\sigma= 1.13\%$ per year, so the terminal standard deviation of the short rate is 1.13% after one year and about 3.57% after ten years. She will use the model to value (i) a 10-year coupon bond and (ii) a 10-year option to buy a long-term bond at a yield of 0%. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Negative rates can be ignored for both securities, because the one-year terminal distribution, three standard deviations either side of 6.18%, does not reach zero.
options.B: At ten years a negative shock of only about 1.73 standard deviations takes the rate below zero; this matters most for the option, which the model overvalues, and much less for the bond.
options.C: At ten years a negative shock of only about 1.73 standard deviations takes the rate below zero; this matters most for the bond, whose value depends on the average rate path, and little for the option.
options.D: The probability of negative rates falls as the horizon lengthens, because the recombining tree pulls the short rate back toward its starting level of 6.18%.

solution:
**Step 1 – Horizon**

At one year, 6.18% is 6.18/1.13 = 5.5 standard deviations above zero: negligible. At ten years, 6.18/3.573 = 1.73 standard deviations.

⇒ A modest negative shock now takes the rate below zero (Figure 1).

**Step 2 – Which security suffers**

The coupon bond depends mostly on the average rate path, so a small probability of negative rates does not rule the model out. The option to buy at a 0% yield is asymmetrically sensitive to very low rates, so the model assigns it much too high a value.

**Interpretation**

Whether negative rates make a model unusable “depends on the application”. This is GARP’s own pair of examples.

**LO:** MR-14 c: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.

- **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.9 (GARP MR Ch.14), Model 1 and Figure 14.1

loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
question: A rates strategist builds a normal short-rate tree and then sets every negative node to zero, following Black’s shadow-rate approach. Which of the following statements about this method is correct?

options.A: The rates in the original tree are the observed rates and the floored rates are the shadow rates, so the shadow rate can never fall below zero.
options.B: When the observed rate reaches zero it can stay there for several periods, until the shadow rate moves back above zero.
options.C: The justification is that aggregate saving and investment decisions can never produce a negative equilibrium rate, so the floor recovers the true rate.
options.D: Flooring changes the dynamics of the rate across the entire range of rates, which is why it is less attractive than switching to a lognormal model.

solution:
**Step 1 – Names**

The original tree holds the shadow rates; the adjusted tree holds the observed rates.

**Step 2 – Dynamics at zero**

When the observed rate hits zero it can remain there until the shadow rate crosses back to a positive value.

⇒ B is GARP’s description.

**Step 3 – Justification**

The observed rate is constrained to be positive only because investors can hold cash; the shadow rate, the result of aggregate saving, investment and consumption, may well be negative.

**Interpretation**

The change from flooring is localised around zero and negative rates; changing the distribution changes dynamics across the entire range.

**LO:** MR-14 c: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.

- **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.9 (GARP MR Ch.14); Black, “Interest Rates as Options”, 1995

loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
question: Rates are close to zero and a desk needs a short-rate model to price interest rate options across a wide range of strikes. One modeller proposes switching from a normal model to a lognormal model to remove negative rates; a colleague proposes keeping the normal model and flooring negative rates at zero. Which assessment is most appropriate?

options.A: The lognormal switch is preferable, because it rules out negative rates without changing the model’s volatility at any level of rates.
options.B: Flooring is preferable here, because its effect is localised around zero, whereas changing the distribution alters rate dynamics, including volatilities, across all rates.
options.C: Neither is needed, because adding time steps to the normal tree makes the terminal distribution continuous and so removes the negative rates.
options.D: The two are equivalent, because any distribution that rules out negative rates has the same volatility structure as a floored normal model.

solution:
**Step 1 – Cost of the lognormal switch**

Building the model around a distribution that rules out negative rates “may result in volatilities that are unacceptable for the purpose at hand”, and it changes dynamics across the entire range of rates, which matters when pricing options at many strikes.

**Step 2 – Cost of the floor**

Only rates near and below zero change.

⇒ With rates close to zero, the floor is the less disruptive fix; Vardeez notes it is preferred in very low-rate environments.

**Interpretation**

The choice depends on purpose. Here the desk prices options across strikes, so it should avoid a fix that distorts volatility at every rate level.

**LO:** MR-14 c: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.

- **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.9 (GARP MR Ch.14); Vardeez notes MR-14 c

question:
A treasury analyst at a Singapore bank uses Model 1 to simulate SGD short rates for its balance sheet. She is preparing a report and must choose one statement on when the possibility of negative rates is most troublesome for this model. Which statement is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “Model 1” is the short-rate process $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ with normally distributed rates and no drift, where $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility and $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

options.A: The probability of negative rates rises with the horizon, because the terminal standard deviation grows with the square root of the horizon, and the problem is more acute when current rates are low.
options.B: The probability of negative rates rises with the horizon, because the terminal standard deviation grows in proportion to the horizon, and the problem is more acute when current rates are low.
options.C: The probability of negative rates falls with the horizon, because more time steps bring the terminal distribution closer to normal, and the problem is more acute when current rates are low.
options.D: The probability of negative rates rises with the horizon, because the terminal standard deviation grows with the square root of the horizon, and the problem does not depend on the level of current rates.

solution:
**When the negative-rate problem is most troublesome**

Stem in one line: most accurate report statement on how horizon and rate level affect negative rates in Model 1.

**Concept and theory**

With no drift, the terminal short rate after $T$ years is normal with mean $r_{0}$ and standard deviation

$\sigma_{T}$ = $\sigma\sqrt{T}$

where $r_{0}$ is the current short rate, $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility and $T$ the horizon in years. Zero lies $r_{0}/\sigma_{T}$ standard deviations below the mean. Two things shrink that distance:

| Driver | Effect on $r_{0}/$($\sigma\sqrt{T}$) | Effect on probability of negative rates |
|---|---|---|
| Longer horizon $T$ | Falls (through $\sqrt{T}$) | Rises |
| Lower current rate $r_{0}$ | Falls (linearly) | Rises |

GARP: over one year the process “will almost certainly not exhibit negative interest rates. The probability . . . however, increases with the horizon.” And: “The challenge of negative rates for term structure models is much more acute, of course, when the current level of rates is low.”

**Applying it to this question**

A correct statement needs three parts: direction with horizon (rises), the mechanism ($\sqrt{T}$ growth of the terminal standard deviation) and the level effect (worse at low rates). Only A has all three.

Stem in one line: which statement comparing distribution change and the zero floor is NOT correct?

The two methods differ in where they change the model. GARP closes the discussion with the comparison: for the floor, “the change, however, is localised around zero and negative rates. Both methods do remove negative rates: lognormal rates “cannot become negative”, and the floored observed rate is by construction never below zero. question:
A junior analyst at a US asset manager is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on how a simple Vasicek tree is turned into a recombining tree. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. The center node on date 2 is fixed first using the drift alone, because the expected perturbation due to volatility over each time step is zero.

II. From each date-1 node the 50% probabilities are replaced by unknown probabilities, ($p,$ 1 $- p$) from the up node and ($q,$ 1 $- q$) from the down node.

III. The up-up rate is then found by adding $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ to the expected rate from the date-1 up node, exactly as in the simple tree.

IV. From the date-2 center node, the date-3 branches are set by adding and subtracting $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ to the expected rate from that node, with probabilities of 50%.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I and III only
options.B: II and IV only
options.C: I, II and III only
options.D: I, II and IV only

GARP’s method (§14.5), in order:

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Keep the first time step as in the simple tree: $r_{0}$ + $k$($\theta- r_{0}$)$dt \pm\sigma\sqrt{dt}$, 50% each. |
| 2 | Fix the date-2 center node by drift alone (expected volatility perturbation is zero), eqs. (14.12) to (14.13). |
| 3 | Replace the date-1 probabilities by unknowns ($p,$ 1$-p$) from the up node and ($q,$ 1$-q$) from the down node; the outer rates $r_{uu}$ and $r_{dd}$ are also unknown. |
| 4 | From each date-1 node, solve the two unknowns so that the tree’s expected rate and standard deviation equal the process’s, eqs. (14.14) to (14.20). |
| 5 | To extend, “begin again at the center”: from the date-2 center node, add and subtract $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ to its expected rate with 50% probabilities, eq. (14.21); then solve the outer date-3 nodes as in step 4. |

mean: $p r_{uu}$ + (1 $- p$) $c$ = $\mu_{u}, \mu_{u}$ = $r_{u}$ + $k$($\theta- r_{u}$) $dt$ (14.16)

question:
A quantitative analyst at a Japanese life insurer is documenting the lower branch of a recombining Vasicek tree for JPY short rates. From the date-1 down node $r_{d}$, the tree moves up to the date-2 center node $c$ with probability $q$, or down to an unknown node $r_{dd}$ with probability 1 $- q$. Define $\mu_{d}$ = $r_{d}$ + $k$($\theta- r_{d}$) $dt$. Which pair of conditions determines $q$ and $r_{dd}$?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, the Vasicek model is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $k$ is the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate in the risk-neutral process, $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility, $dt$ the time step in years and $dw$ a normal random variable with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$. Rates are in percent.

options.A: $q c$ + (1 $- q$) $r_{dd}$ = $r_{d}$ and $\sqrt{q \text{(}c - r_{d}\text{)}^{2} \text{+ (1} - q\text{) (}r_{dd} - r_{d}\text{)}^{2}}$ = $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$
options.B: $q c$ + (1 $- q$) $r_{dd}$ = $\mu_{d}$ and $\sqrt{q \text{(}c - \mu_{d}\text{)}^{2} \text{+ (1} - q\text{) (}r_{dd} - \mu_{d}\text{)}^{2}}$ = $\sigma$
options.C: $q c$ + (1 $- q$) $r_{dd}$ = $\mu_{d}$ and $\sqrt{q \text{(}c - \mu_{d}\text{)}^{2} \text{+ (1} - q\text{) (}r_{dd} - \mu_{d}\text{)}^{2}}$ = $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$
options.D: $q r_{dd}$ + (1 $- q$) $c$ = $\mu_{d}$ and $\sqrt{q \text{(}r_{dd} - \mu_{d}\text{)}^{2} \text{+ (1} - q\text{) (}c - \mu_{d}\text{)}^{2}}$ = $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$

solution:
**The two conditions for the down branch**

Stem in one line: from the date-1 down node, up to $c$ with probability $q$, down to $r_{dd}$ with 1 $- q$; which pair of conditions determines $q$ and $r_{dd}$?

**Concept and theory**

The down branch mirrors the up branch. GARP: the expected rate from 4.7786% is 4.7786% + $\frac{.025}{12}$ (15.339% − 4.7786%) = 4.8006% (14.18), and the standard deviation is again 36.37 bp. Then

$q \times$ 5.1635% + (1 $- q$) $\times r_{dd}$ = 4.8006% (14.19)

$\sqrt{q \text{(5}.\text{1635\%} - 4.\text{8006\%)}^{2} \text{+ (1} - q\text{) (}r_{dd} - 4.\text{8006\%)}^{2}}$ = .3637% (14.20)

giving $r_{dd}$ = 4.4361% and $q$ = .5011. In general symbols, with $\mu_{d}$ = $r_{d}$ + $k$($\theta- r_{d}$)$dt$:

$q c$ + (1 $- q$) $r_{dd}$ = $\mu_{d}, \sqrt{q \text{(}c - \mu_{d}\text{)}^{2} \text{+ (1} - q\text{) (}r_{dd} - \mu_{d}\text{)}^{2}}$ = $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$

Each condition has three ingredients that must be right: the probability attached to the right node, the centre $\mu_{d}$ (not $r_{d}$), and the one-step standard deviation $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem defines $q$ as the probability of moving up to $c$. Only C attaches $q$ to $c$, centres both conditions on $\mu_{d}$, and uses $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$.
